summary: Describes the Certificate Request Message Format (CRMF), a standard way to structure a request for an X.509 certificate sent to a certification authority. It was replaced by RFC 4211.

eli5.summary: When you ask for a digital ID card you fill in a form. This document defines what that form looks like so every issuing office can read it.

questions: how do you request an x.509 certificate
what is proof of possession in certificates
subtitle: Standard format for asking a certification authority to issue an X.509 certificate.

tldr.problem: Organizations and people need digital certificates issued by a Certification Authority, but there was no standard format for the request message. This meant different CAs expected different structures, making it hard to build compatible software.
tldr.mechanism: CRMF defines a standard message format that includes the public key being certified, the requested certificate details, proof that the requester owns the corresponding private key, and optional registration information such as contact details.
tldr.outcome: Certificate authorities and clients can now speak the same language when requesting certificates. RFC 4211 replaced this specification with improvements.

facts.label: Core components
facts.value: CertRequest, Proof of Possession, Registration Info

today: RFC 4211 replaced this specification in 2005 with an improved and clarified version of the certificate request message format.

sections.title: Why CRMF Exists
sections.content:
A Certification Authority (CA) issues digital certificates that bind a person or organization's name to their public key. When an entity wants a certificate, it must request one from a CA. Before CRMF, there was no standard format for such requests, so different CAs expected different message structures and different information.

The Certificate Request Message Format solves this by defining a standard syntax for requesting a certificate. It specifies what fields must or may be included, what order they come in, and how to encode them. A request includes the public key to be certified, the name or names the certificate should bear, the requested validity period, and other certificate details. Equally important, the requester must prove that they own the private key that goes with the public key, to prevent someone else from requesting a certificate for your key.
sections.eli5: Before this, every certificate office had its own form. CRMF is the universal form everyone agrees on.

sections.title: The Structure of a Certificate Request
sections.content:
A CRMF message consists of three optional or required parts:

1. The CertRequest. This is the core: the public key being certified, the end-entity's name (or names), serial number if desired, signature algorithm, validity dates, and any X.509 extensions the certificate should carry (such as key usage restrictions or subject alternative names). It may also include controls that affect how the request is processed (such as a registration token or instructions for publishing the certificate).

2. Proof of Possession. A field in which the requester demonstrates that they have the private key corresponding to the public key in the request. The exact format depends on the type of key (signature, encryption, or key agreement). For a signature key, the proof is a signature over the request. For encryption and key agreement keys, the proof may be a challenge-response exchange or decryption of a value. This prevents an attacker from requesting a certificate for someone else's key.

3. Registration Information. Optional supplementary data such as subscriber contact information, billing information, or other details needed to fulfill the request. This is kept separate from the certificate content itself, because information in this field does not become part of the certificate.
sections.eli5: A certificate request has three parts: what you want (your key and name), proof you have the key, and extra info like your phone number.

sections.title: Proof of Possession and Key Types
sections.content:
Proof of Possession (POP) is the critical mechanism that prevents impersonation. Without POP, an attacker could request a certificate for Alice's public key without Alice's knowledge, and the CA would have no way to detect the fraud.

The method of proving possession differs by key type:

  • Signature keys: The requester signs some data (such as the request itself or a random value) using the private key. The CA verifies the signature using the public key in the request. If the signature is valid, the requester must have the private key.
  • Encryption keys: The CA may issue a challenge (a random value) that the requester must decrypt and return, proving they have the decryption key. Alternatively, the CA can send an encrypted certificate that only the intended recipient can decrypt, and the requester proves possession by demonstrating they can decrypt it.
  • Key agreement keys (Diffie-Hellman): The requester and CA establish a shared secret by combining their Diffie-Hellman values, then compute a message authentication code over the request using that secret. The CA performs the same computation and verifies the codes match.

A CA or Registration Authority is responsible for enforcing proof of possession by some means. Some CAs may verify it in the message itself; others may use out-of-band methods (such as confirming the request by email or telephone). What matters is that the CA does not issue a certificate without verifying that the requester has the private key.
sections.eli5: When you ask for a certificate, you prove you have the secret key by using it in a special way only you can do. Different kinds of keys have different ways to prove it.

sections.title: Controls and Registration Options
sections.content:
A CertRequest may include controls that affect how the CA or RA processes the request. Some examples:

  • Registration Token: A one-time password or credential provided out of band by the CA, which the requester includes in the request. The CA verifies it before issuing the certificate.
  • Authenticator: Knowledge-based or other non-cryptographic proof of identity, such as the answer to a security question, a personal ID number, or a hash thereof.
  • Publication Information: Instructions on whether and where the CA should publish the issued certificate (in a directory, on a web page, in LDAP, etc.).
  • Archive Options: Indicates whether and how the CA should archive a copy of the private key (used only when the CA generates the key on behalf of the requester).
  • Old Certificate ID: If this is a renewal or replacement request, identifies which old certificate is being replaced.
  • Protocol Encryption Key: A public key the CA may use to encrypt sensitive information in its response.

The request may also include registration information (regInfo) such as subscriber name, email address, job title, billing details, or other data relevant to the organization issuing the certificate. This information becomes part of the request but not of the certificate itself.
sections.eli5: You can include extra instructions with your request, like 'use this password', 'publish this certificate', or 'here's my phone number'.

sections.title: Security and Obsolescence
sections.content:
The security of CRMF depends on the secure transport of the message to the CA and on proper enforcement of proof of possession. The RFC itself does not define how the request reaches the CA; that is the responsibility of the protocol carrying it (such as HTTPS or a dedicated certificate enrollment protocol).

Encryption of the request is strongly recommended if it contains sensitive information and the CA has a known encryption certificate. Proof of possession MUST be validated by some means, because without it the entire purpose of the PKI is compromised.

RFC 4211 obsoleted this specification and provides an updated certificate request message format.
sections.eli5: Keep the request private and always check the proof of possession. A newer version exists now.
